name: Rizpah
charge: Spreading sackcloth on the rock and suffering neither the birds by day nor the beasts by night to touch the bodies
summary: Seven of Saul's sons were given to the Gibeonites and hanged in the hill before the Lord in the beginning of barley harvest. Two of them were hers. She took sackcloth and spread it on the rock and stayed from the beginning of harvest until water dropped on them out of heaven, keeping the birds off by day and the beasts off by night. It was told David, and he took the bones of Saul and Jonathan and of those seven and buried them in the sepulchre of Kish.
offense: Two of Rizpah's sons were among the seven delivered to the Gibeonites in the judgment concerning Saul's bloody house. From the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon the bodies from heaven, she spread sackcloth upon the rock and kept the birds away by day and the beasts by night (2 Samuel 21:8-10). She could not restore her sons to life, but she would not abandon their bodies to be consumed. Her watch extended beyond an hour of mourning. Day and night brought different threats, and she remained attentive to both. The account records her action without placing a speech in her mouth. Her perseverance itself made the condition of the dead known. The law required care even for the body of a man put to death and hanged, forbidding it to remain upon the tree overnight and defile the land (Deuteronomy 21:22-23). The exposure in this account was prolonged; Rizpah's vigil did not substitute for burial. It preserved the bodies until the matter reached the king and burial followed.
judgment: David was told what Rizpah had done. He went to gather the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead and gathered the bones of those who had been hanged (2 Samuel 21:11-13). The response reached beyond her two sons to the earlier dead of Saul's house. The bones of Saul and Jonathan were buried in the sepulchre of Kish, and all that the king commanded was performed. Afterward God was entreated for the land (2 Samuel 21:14). The account closes not with the bodies exposed upon the hill, but with burial and the land's relief. Rizpah's sons were not returned to her. The good that followed her endurance was the care given to the dead and the completion of a matter affecting the whole land. Her vigil stands within the record of judgment as an act of steadfast attention to those who could no longer speak for themselves.
